claimSlots.statement: No single physical examination test can be recommended to make a definitive diagnosis of a specific shoulder condition, and the evidence on these tests is largely low quality.

candidateSources.citation: Zhao Q, Palani P, Kassab NS, et al. Evidence-based approach to the shoulder examination for subacromial bursitis and rotator cuff tears: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC Musculoskelet Disord. 2024;25(1):1028.

Hegedus EJ, Goode AP, Cook CE, et al. Which physical examination tests provide clinicians with the most value when examining the shoulder? Update of a systematic review with meta-analysis of individual tests. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46(14):964-978.

claimSlots.note: Zhao 2024 is open (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0) and is the primary source; Hegedus 2012 concludes that no single test can be recommended for a definitive diagnosis and is kept as a bounded historical example.

scenarios.prompt: After a fall in class, the shoulder looks out of place.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Emergency: call emergency services; do not move the arm or try to put it back.

scenarios.prompt: After catching a heavy bar: pain and weakness lifting the arm; it still moves and looks normal.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Urgent: stop; urgent GP or NHS 111 today.

scenarios.prompt: Pins and needles in the arm that have not gone away.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Urgent: stop; urgent GP or NHS 111 today.

scenarios.prompt: A mild ache after last week's pressing that settled within a day; no pain during sets; no warning signs.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Continue; consider load or range for this session; stop if pain comes on during a set.

scenarios.prompt: Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks of leaving out the provoking movements.
A 16-year-old says the shoulder hurts after training.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Urgent: stop shoulder loading; tell a parent or carer; GP or NHS 111 the same day for referral to trauma and orthopaedics.

lesson.title: Assessments, screens and red flags
lesson.summary: Screens show a trainer where to look and when to stop. They never diagnose and never clear anyone. Learn three simple screens, the questions to ask first, and the warning signs that end the session.
objectives: Ask the questions that bring warning signs to light before you train the shoulder.
Run three simple screens, each with a clear start position and what to look for.
Explain why a trainer's screen can neither diagnose nor clear a shoulder.
Choose the right referral tier from what you see and hear.

blocks.content: A screen is a short, repeatable look at how a shoulder moves today. It helps you choose a starting point and notice change. It is not a test, and it is never the reason someone is allowed to train.
What a screen is, and is not
Even in clinicians' hands, no single physical examination test can be recommended for diagnosing a specific shoulder condition on its own, and much of the research on these tests is low in quality.
A trainer's screen is simpler still. It shows how a movement looks today. It never diagnoses, it never clears anyone for training, and a "normal" screen does not outweigh a warning sign.

content: Did anything happen to the shoulder recently: a fall, an impact, a joint that popped out?
Any pins and needles, numbness or loss of feeling in the arm or hand?
Is there anything you cannot do with the arm that you could do recently, like lifting it yourself?
Does it hurt at night, or is it getting worse?
Do you have a fever or feel unwell? Any chest pain or breathlessness?
Is a doctor or physiotherapist treating this shoulder or your neck, or have you had surgery on it?
For younger clients: are you under 18?

content.label: Emergency
content.text: Emergency: call emergency services now. Arm pain with chest pain, tightness or breathlessness, or the client collapses. After a fall or impact, an arm they cannot move or a shoulder that looks out of place: do not move the arm or try to put it back, and do not let them drive. A shoulder that is suddenly very painful and red or warm, or fever or feeling unwell with shoulder pain. If more than one applies, the highest tier wins.

content.label: Urgent
content.text: Urgent: an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 today (or the local equivalent). Sudden or very bad pain. A new inability to lift or move the arm themselves, without an injury. Pain and weakness after an injury while the arm still moves. Any other new pain after an injury or a fall. Changed shape or bad swelling with no injury. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling. An arm that feels hot or cold. Severe pain in both shoulders. A new lump. Several joints newly painful or swollen. Anyone under 18 with shoulder pain: tell a parent or carer; GP or NHS 111 the same day. If more than one applies, the highest tier wins.

content.label: Routine
content.text: Routine: a GP or physiotherapist. Pain that is getting worse: refer now, without waiting. Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks. Movement that is very difficult but still possible. Pain and stiffness that do not go away, including pain at night. Pain that stays after you have removed the movements that provoke it. If more than one applies, the highest tier wins.

content.label: Outside this module
content.text: Recent surgery or a recent dislocation or fracture still in rehabilitation, a diagnosed neurological condition, or a diagnosed shoulder condition under current care: work only within the treating clinician's plan, and do not progress it on your own. Anyone under 18 with shoulder pain: urgent, as above.

content: Start: the client stands relaxed, arms by the sides, in a top that lets you see the shoulder blades. Stand behind them.
Ask them to raise both arms forward and up as far as is comfortable, then lower slowly. Three to five times.
Look for: how high each arm goes, whether both shoulder blades move at a similar time and amount, and whether one lifts away from the ribs on the way down.
A side-to-side difference tells you where to look in training. It does not tell you why.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Stop the screen, and stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session, if pain comes on or rises. If the client cannot lift the arm themselves and there was no injury: urgent, today. After a fall or impact, an arm they cannot move or a shoulder that looks out of place: emergency, now. Pins and needles that do not go away: urgent, today. This screen never clears anyone and never names an injury.

content: Start: the client stands with the elbow at the side, bent to a right angle, thumb up.
Ask them to turn the forearm outward, then inward across the body, without moving the elbow. Compare sides.
Then, if comfortable, with the arm out to the side at shoulder height and the elbow bent, ask them to rotate the hand up and down. Compare sides.
The client moves the arm; you do not push it.
For throwing athletes, read lesson 7 before drawing any conclusion from a difference between sides.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Stop the screen, and stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session, if pain comes on or rises. Weakness with pain after an injury, while the arm still moves: urgent, today. A new inability to turn or lift the arm themselves: urgent, today. Pain that is getting worse over the following days: routine referral now. This screen never clears anyone and never names an injury.

content: Start: the client stands relaxed.
Reach over the shoulder to touch the upper back, one side at a time. Note where the fingertips reach.
Reach behind the back and up the spine, one side at a time. Note where the thumb reaches.
Compare sides, and compare with last time.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: Stop the screen, and stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session, if pain comes on or rises. Stiffness or pain that has not improved after 2 weeks, or pain at night with stiffness that does not go away: routine referral. Severe pain in both shoulders, or several joints newly painful or swollen: urgent, today. This screen never clears anyone and never names an injury.

blocks.content: What to do with what you saw

Write down what you saw in plain words, without a diagnosis. Then choose: train as planned, adjust the plan for the next session, or refer, and say which tier. Re-check the same screen the same way in a later session.

When you refer, keep it calm and specific: "I noticed you can't lift your arm as high as last week and it's new. That's worth getting checked today by a GP or NHS 111. We'll work on your lower body for the rest of the session." Do not name a condition, and do not say it is nothing.

content.prompt: Can a trainer use one screen to diagnose a shoulder problem or to clear a shoulder for training?
options: Yes, if the screen is done carefully
No: even clinicians' single tests cannot identify a condition on their own
Only if the client has no pain
content.explanation: No single examination test identifies a specific shoulder condition, even for clinicians; a trainer's screen never diagnoses and never clears anyone.

content.prompt: What is the quality of the research on clinicians' physical examination tests for common shoulder conditions?
content.explanation: A 2024 systematic review described a large body of low-quality evidence for these tests.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: Pick the tier for each, and say what you do first: (1) after a fall in class, the shoulder looks out of place; (2) after catching a heavy bar, pain and weakness lifting the arm, but it still moves and looks normal; (3) pins and needles in the arm that have not gone away; (4) a mild ache after last week's pressing that settled within a day, with no pain during sets; (5) pain that has not improved after 2 weeks of leaving out the movements that provoke it; (6) a 16-year-old says the shoulder hurts after training.
